job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Colin Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now my day is half applications and half building a thing. I share a room above a pizzeria in Port Sellick with two other guys, so I smell garlic from nine in the morning. I use an AI assistant to tailor each application and to practise interview questions, then in the afternoon I work on a little budgeting tool for freelancers that has forty users and earns me roughly nothing yet. I finished business and finance at Aldermoor University, top of the year, with internships at a payments start-up and the finance team of a logistics firm. Six months of searching, a few second interviews, no offer, and 39,000 of debt, which is why I take weekend gigs doing data entry for a printer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd say fair enough, it was always going to settle down. I'd tell people it's a good tool and a bad religion. I'd go on using it exactly as I do now, because it already saves me about an hour a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a plateau doesn't help me. I have debt, I'm one month from running out of money, and the market near Port Sellick is thin. I'd be fine in the long run, but the next six months are the squeeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd widen the net to the big cities and take a contract role if there was one. I'd keep the printer gigs and try to turn the budgeting tool into at least a few hundred a month. I'd also say yes to anything that gives me a reference, even if it's not exactly the job I wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit frustrated, but not hopeless. I like having something to build, so I can keep busy and keep my head clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say the garlic smell starts at nine. How long can you keep this up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd see what ten months looks like, honestly. I can keep it up on the gigs and the room rent I pay split three ways, but I can't do it for much longer than that. If nothing comes, I'd move to a bigger city, sleep on a friend's floor and take whatever's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want a first employer to offer you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Training, a mentor and real work in the first week. I'd take less pay for a place where I learn, because experience is the currency here, and I'd say so to a recruiter.

I'd carry on using it as now, since it saves about an **hour** a day.
think: A plateau doesn't help me: **debt**, one month of money and a thin local market.
I'd be fine in the long run, but the next six months are the **squeeze**.
do: Widen the search to big **cities** and take a contract role if offered.
Keep the printer gigs and aim to earn a few hundred a month from my **budgeting tool**.
Accept any role that gives me a **reference**.
feel: **Frustrated** but not hopeless, since building something keeps my head clear.

fieldNote: Treats AI as a plain tool and builds on it, which reflects his **adaptive** side.

Willing to trade pay for **learning**, which signals confidence in himself.

Sleep on a friend's floor in a bigger city if an offer comes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening and it's a chance, but only for people who prepare. At my age everyone is hearing different things, so I'd show friends what I do with it, step by step. I'd tell them to pick one tool and use it for a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's good and bad for me. It means fewer entry-level seats, since the first-year-analyst work gets done by software. But the people who can run the software and talk to customers are the ones firms want, and that's the group I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn the budgeting tool into a real product, with a free level and a paid one, and chase fifty paying users in a year. I'd apply for roles that mention data, automation or operations, where a finance person who understands the tools is rare. And I'd go to the monthly meetups in the city and talk to the people who are hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pumped, to be honest, but with a nervous edge. If it goes wrong I've got debts and no safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use these tools every day. What is the next thing they'll take over in finance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reconciliation, reporting, first-draft forecasts. At the logistics firm the monthly report used to take two analysts three days and a script cut it to an afternoon. The people who built the script got promoted, and I want to be one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you not want to be in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The person who does the same task in the same way for fifteen years and doesn't look up. That person gets surprised, and I'd rather be the one who is looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not prepared, and the people who say they are, are guessing. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen, and I'd be asking what the plan is for people with loans. I'd also say, quietly, that there's a lot of opportunity if you move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think everything turns on the next twelve months. I'd see a window where the people who know the tools can still earn, and then a drop. My adaptability helps for a year, but a machine adapts faster than I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on building and selling something now, not later. I'd move my savings and any wages to a safe place, and I'd pay down the loan with every spare cent. I'd also look for hands-on routes, like operating or fixing robots, since those come in later and someone has to oversee them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A rush, honestly. Scared and excited together, like standing on a high board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. Does your adaptability help, or does it run out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My adaptability helps and then it runs out. For a year I'm ahead of most people, and then everyone has the same tools, so my advantage shrinks. That's why I'd try to have a business that doesn't depend on one skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the budgeting tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to sell it to a bank or a payroll firm, or get a few hundred paying users and show it earns. If it gets bought for even a modest sum, it pays the loan. It's a long shot, but long shots are worth taking when everything else is shaky.

steps.text: Sell the budgeting tool to a bank or payroll firm
Chase a few hundred paying users to show it earns
Put every spare cent at the student loan
Learn how to run and fix warehouse robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift for anyone who uses it. I'd tell my friends to start building now and not wait for permission. I'd be bold in public, because the loud, early people get hired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel pretty good. I could get a first job in finance in the next year, work it for three, and have a business or a better role to go to before the big shift. Most importantly, I'd have about 25,000 of the loan paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any decent first job, learn the real systems, and keep the budgeting tool going on evenings. By year two I'd have moved into an automation role, since that's where finance people with tech skills are scarce. I'd be paying 500 a month at the loan and saving the same again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Optimistic with a sense of urgency. Five years is enough but not so much that I can drift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. Where would you be by 2029?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2029 I'd be working in an automation or product role at a finance firm, with the side product earning something. I'd probably be in a big city and renting my own place, which feels like a milestone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your mum and dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents, who run a small garage, would say be careful and put money aside. They'd also be impressed that I'm working on something of my own, even if they don't quite follow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the future looks big and a bit strange, and that anyone with ten years should be curious. I'd tell friends to try new things each year. I'd be public about what I'm building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel good, honestly. With ten years, even a mistake is survivable. I'd have time to try a business, fail at it and still be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a first job, learn the field, then try to launch a proper product by year three. I'd clear the loan by year six and start putting money into shares. I'd also be learning each new tool as it lands, because that's what keeps me ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little greedy for what's possible. Ten years is a lot of runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is long. Do you worry that you'd get complacent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might, yes, which is why I'd set a rule that every year I learn a new skill. Complacency kills careers, and I have a habit of jumping when things get quiet, which I'd use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you invest anything you earned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Index funds first, then a bit in a small business or two I believe in. I'd keep a six-month cushion, since the one thing I know is that things change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two year one. I'd have a year of advantage and then a cliff, and with a loan and no savings, I'd be racing. What would help is a quick loan pause, small grants for people starting things, and firms that tell juniors what they actually need.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that adaptable doesn't mean safe. I'm good with change and I still lie awake about the loan. I'd like someone to say that the grads who try things aren't fine just because we look fine.

headlineQuote: Adaptable doesn't mean safe. I'm good with change and I still lie awake about the loan.
portrait: Colin is 23, top of his business and finance class, in a **shared room** above a pizzeria with 39,000 of debt.
He uses AI daily, builds a budgeting tool for freelancers and does weekend data entry for a printer.
Centrist and quick to act, he takes risks and sees himself on the **builder** side of any change.
His mood is anxious in the fast worlds and calm in the slow ones, but the loan always weighs on him.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario, because his tool-skill edge would last about a year, then a cliff.
whatWouldHelp: A fast **loan pause**, small grants for people starting businesses, and firms being clear about what juniors need.
